chunks.text: Neem, Azadirachta indica, is a fast-growing Meliaceae tree native to the Indian subcontinent and parts of Indochina, typically 15-20 m tall (rarely to 35-40 m) with a dense rounded crown, pinnate leaves of 20-30 leaflets, fragrant white flowers in large drooping panicles, and olive-like fruit. It is prized for drought tolerance and is valued for anti-desertification planting and possibly as a carbon sink, though it has become an invasive weed in parts of the Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa and northern Australia (declared a Class B/C weed in Australia's Northern Territory in 2015). Its seed oil yields azadirachtin, identified in the 1960s as a potent natural insect antifeedant and growth disruptor still used today as a biopesticide. Culturally it is deeply woven into Indian life: the Vaishnava saint Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's name 'Nimai' means 'born under a neem tree', neem twigs are used as traditional teeth-cleaning sticks, and its flowers and shoots are eaten in regional dishes such as Tamil neem-flower rasam and Bengali nim begun bhaja. Despite extensive traditional and Ayurvedic use, Wikipedia is careful to flag that clinical evidence for most claimed medicinal benefits remains insufficient, and that neem oil is actually toxic to small children and can cause death.

chunks.source: Down To Earth — 'Back where it belongs' (neem patent revocation)
chunks.text: This report lays out the landmark 1990s-2000s neem biopiracy dispute in detail. In 1994 the European Patent Office granted the US Department of Agriculture and the US chemical company W.R. Grace a patent (No. 0436257) on a 'hydrophobic extracted neem oil' as a novel fungicide, building on an earlier 1992 Grace patent on extracting and stabilising azadirachtin. A coalition formed in 1995 — the Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology (RFSTE) in New Delhi, the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements, and former MEP Magda Aelvoet, backed by NGOs from 40 countries — filed a formal opposition, arguing the patent lacked an inventive step because neem's fungicidal properties had been public knowledge in India for centuries. After a two-day oral hearing in Munich, the EPO's Opposition Division revoked the patent on 11 May 2000, with witnesses Abhay Phadke and U.B. Singh providing evidence of prior traditional use; Indian minister Murli Manohar Joshi publicly called the original patent 'biopiracy'. (The patentees later appealed, and Wikipedia reports the EPO's Technical Board of Appeal finally dismissed that appeal and upheld the revocation on 8 March 2005 — so the case has two important dates depending on whether one counts the original 2000 ruling or the final 2005 appellate confirmation.) At the time, roughly 40 further neem-related patent applications remained pending before the EPO out of close to 90 such patents filed worldwide, underscoring how commercially contested neem-derived compounds had become.
